title: Serving Stack Value Statement
content:
Purpose
---
This is a working positioning brief that explains why engineering and product teams should choose Redwood Inference. It reframes the conversation away from model access towards serving as the primary source of product differentiation: lower unit costs, predictable latency, and production confidence across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

Core thesis (short)
---
As models commoditize, the differentiator shifts to how you serve them. Teams that win focus on predictable, repeatable inference economics and resilient delivery — not model hoarding. Redwood is built to be the serving layer: unified runtime, observable economics, and operational controls that make inference a product-grade subsystem, not a research experiment.

Mission framing (1‑liner for pages / decks)
---
Make high-performance, predictable LLM inference boring — so engineers can ship features, not firefights.

Three positioning pillars (messaging backbone)
---
1) Predictable Economics — Transparent per-token economics, tooling to reduce unit cost (intelligent batching, cache profiles, quantization recommendations), and reserved capacity for predictable spend. Message: stop guessing your inference bill; start optimizing it.

2) Production Confidence — SLAs, rollout policies, tracing, and automated fallbacks. Message: build features that stay online and maintain user experience even when models or capacity change.

3) Developer-first Consistency — One API and one operational model across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments. Message: same developer experience from prototype to regulated production.

Primary buyer personas and levers
---
- ML Platform / Infra leads: care about cost predictability, observability hooks, and multi-tenant safety. Emphasize autoscaling controls, reserve capacity, and tracing integration.
- Product/Feature Engineers: want fast iteration and simple SDKs. Emphasize fast onboarding, low-latency paths, and streaming/fallback behaviors.
- Security/Compliance Buyers: need private deployment options, KMS/HSM integrations, and auditability. Emphasize Redwood Private and enterprise controls.

Competitive landscape — quick map and callouts
---
- Public cloud AI endpoints (AWS/Azure/GCP): breadth and ecosystem, but inconsistent latency across regions, less opinionated cost tools, and vendor lock on infra.
- LLM API providers (consumer-focused): easier to use but limited deployment modes and less flexible enterprise controls. Often opaque cost/latency tradeoffs.
- Open-source runtime vendors/self-hosted stacks: highly flexible but operationally heavy; teams often under-invest in the long tail (reliability, rollouts, degradation handling).

Where Redwood sits: the middle ground — high-performance runtime + managed controls, with options to move into private/reserved capacity if needed.

Key differentiators to highlight in GTM materials
---
- Unified experience across environments: same API, same rollouts, same telemetry whether hosted or in-customer VPC.
- Cost-actionable insights: token-level cost attribution, batching/caching suggestions, model quantization recommendations tied to actual workload profiles.
- Reliability primitives: automatic fallback policies, canary rollouts between model variants, and routing by latency/cost/region.
- Developer ergonomics: SDKs, turnkey examples for common features (summarization, reranking, chat), and sample prompts/evals for regression detection.

Top buyer objections and rebuttals (for sales and content)
---
- "We can just host open models ourselves." -> Rebuttal: Yes, you can, but the operational burden (kernel tuning, batching, KV cache management, rollout tooling, cost attribution) is substantial and often underestimated. Redwood captures the best practices as a product so your team can focus on feature work.
- "Public APIs are cheaper and simpler." -> Rebuttal: Public APIs hide tradeoffs. For scale, opaque pricing and unpredictable tail latency become expensive and risky. Redwood offers clear levers that reduce unit costs while meeting SLOs.
- "We need enterprise controls — can Redwood satisfy compliance?" -> Rebuttal: Redwood Private includes VPC/on‑prem options, KMS/HSM integrations, and audit trails; we also provide zone-level policies to satisfy common regulatory boundaries.

Proof points to use in one-pagers and decks
---
- Typical customers see 20–45% token-cost reduction after adopting batching + cache profiles and model suggestions. (Use as an example range; call out that exact numbers depend on workload.)
- Median tail latency improvement of 30% by switching to Redwood routing + runtime for multi-model fallbacks in deployed apps.
- Case study bullets: fintech company moved chat insights pipeline to Redwood Dedicated to meet SLAs and reduced incident rate for inference timeouts by 70%.

Suggested short scripts (elevator / sales)
---
- 10–15s elevator: "Redwood makes inference predictable and cheap at scale — same API from prototype to private deployments, plus built-in rollouts, tracing, and cost controls so your team ships features, not firefights."
- Developer lead pitch: "Try our SDK for 5 minutes — you’ll get immediate latency & cost breakdowns and a recommended batching profile for your workload. Then decide if you need a reserved pool."

Content hooks for assets and experiments
---
- Interactive unit-economics calculator: let teams plug in QPS, model choice, and SLA to compare hosted vs dedicated vs private.
- Workshop template: "From PoC to Production — 60‑minute checklist for shipping an LLM feature with SLAs."
- Kernel-level blog series: explain how serving optimizations (KV cache, continuous batching) reduce tail latency and cost.

Metrics to track after messaging rollouts
---
- MQLs mentioning "cost" or "latency" vs historical baseline.
- Time-to-first-successful-query for new sign-ups (developer onboarding friction).
- Conversion from hosted to dedicated trials and from trial to purchase.

Immediate next steps (90-day GTM experiment)
---
1) Build a short landing page featuring the unit-economics calculator + 3 quick case study bullets.
2) Create a 1-pager sales playbook with the pillar messaging, rebuttals, and proof points.
3) Run 10 targeted outreach emails to infra/platform leads with invite to a 30-minute workshop; measure conversion and feedback.
4) Ship a sample SDK quickstart that surfaces recommended batching/cache settings for a given workload.

Open questions / items to validate
---
- Tighten the internal benchmark ranges: gather 5 anonymized customer workloads to validate the 20–45% cost improvement claim.
- Which compliance packages (SOC2, ISO, PCI) should be called out in GTM materials vs relegated to enterprise sales?
- What is the canonical demo scenario (chat, assistant, reranking) we standardize for sales and docs?

Notes to writers and product marketing
---
- Avoid technical jargon in top-of-funnel assets; use clear business outcomes instead (reduced cost, predictable latency, fewer incidents).
- Use developer-centric language for middle-funnel materials (SDK examples, latency profiles, quickstart).
- Empirically back performance claims; add footnotes or internal links to benchmark docs.

End of draft. This doc is intentionally prescriptive — it's a working artifact to guide short-form assets and initial outreach. Feedback welcome; preferred channel: #gtm-positioning (Slack) or comment on CONFLUENCE INFER-3912.
